title: Overlapping instructions to finish more
objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain what a pipeline overlaps, compute the speedup it offers and the limit on that speedup, and say what a deeper pipeline costs.

blocks.text: In the multi-cycle design, an instruction uses one stage at a time and the other four sit idle. A pipeline fills them: while instruction one is in execute, instruction two is in decode and instruction three is being fetched. Nothing about a single instruction gets faster — but instructions complete far more often.

blocks.caption: Five instructions in flight, one completing per cycle
lines: instr 1   | IF  | ID  | EX  | MEM | WB  |
instr 2         | IF  | ID  | EX  | MEM | WB  |
instr 3               | IF  | ID  | EX  | MEM | WB  |
After cycle 5, one instruction completes every cycle.
Each one still takes 5 cycles from start to finish.

blocks.title: Latency unchanged, throughput multiplied
blocks.text: Each instruction still takes five cycles from fetch to write-back — its latency is identical. What changed is that five instructions are in progress at once, so after the pipeline fills, one finishes every cycle. This is the same distinction as a production line: making one item takes just as long, and the factory produces far more of them.

blocks.caption: Computing the gain for a real number of instructions
lines: Without a pipeline: 1000 instructions x 5 cycles      = 5000 cycles
4 cycles to fill, then one instruction per cycle
/* The ceiling is the number of stages: 5 stages can at best give 5x.
With 1000 instructions the fill cost is negligible; with 10 it is not:
4 + 10 = 14 cycles against 50, which is 3.6x — the same pipeline,
a much smaller gain, because filling it dominated. */

blocks.text: Why not simply add more stages

rows: A shorter stage, so a faster clock
A longer fill, so short bursts benefit less
More instructions in flight to be discarded when a branch is mispredicted
More places where one instruction needs another's unfinished result
Storage between every pair of stages, which itself costs time

blocks.text: Processor designs pushed pipelines to great depth in pursuit of clock speed, and then retreated. The reason is the second row: when a branch is guessed wrongly, everything after it in the pipeline must be thrown away, and a deeper pipeline throws away more. That trade is the subject of the hazard module.

blocks.title: The picture above is the ideal case, and it is not what happens
blocks.text: It assumes every instruction can proceed every cycle. Three things break that: an instruction needing a result the previous one has not produced yet, a load whose value is not back in time, and a branch whose direction is not yet known. Each has a name and a remedy, and the next three lessons are those three cases. The pipeline is easy; the exceptions are the subject.
What has to be true for this to work

items: Every stage must take the same time, or the slowest one sets the rate for all
Stages must not need the same hardware at the same time — which is why instruction and data memory are separate paths
Each stage must carry its instruction's information forward, since the stage before it now holds a different instruction
Instructions must be easy to decode without knowing what came before — the fixed-length argument from the first module, paid off here

blocks.text: That last point is where the RISC-versus-CISC argument finally lands. A variable-length instruction cannot be fetched independently, because you cannot know where it starts without decoding the one before it. Pipelining it is possible — modern x86-64 processors do it — but only by decoding into simpler internal operations first, which is the extra machinery the earlier lesson described.

blocks.title: Compute and compare
steps: For 100 instructions on a 5-stage pipeline, compute the cycles and the speedup
Do the same for 10 instructions and explain why the speedup is so much lower
For a 20-stage pipeline with 1000 instructions, compute the cycles
If the deeper pipeline also allows a 2x faster clock, compare the total times
Now assume 10% of instructions are branches and 25% of those are mispredicted, discarding the whole pipeline each time
Recompute both pipelines with that cost included, and say which now wins
Explain in one sentence why processor designs stopped getting deeper
Read: sysctl -a 2>/dev/null | grep -i cpu | head -5    or lscpu, and note what your machine reports
blocks.expected: A speedup that approaches the stage count for long runs and falls well short for short ones, and a deep pipeline that loses once mispredictions are included. That final calculation is the argument that ended the pursuit of ever-deeper pipelines, and doing it yourself is more convincing than being told.

cheatsheet: A pipeline overlaps stages of different instructions, filling units that would idle
Latency per instruction is unchanged; throughput approaches one per cycle
Speedup ceiling is the number of stages; 1000 instructions on 5 stages gives 4.98x
For short runs, filling the pipeline dominates: 10 instructions give only 3.6x
Deeper pipelines allow a faster clock but discard more work on a misprediction
Every stage must take the same time, or the slowest sets the rate
Instruction and data memory are separate paths so two stages can use memory at once
Fixed-length instructions can be fetched without decoding the previous one
The ideal picture assumes no instruction ever waits — the next lessons are the exceptions

checkpoint.prompt: A 5-stage pipeline is running. How long does one instruction take from fetch to write-back?

choices.B: Five cycles — its latency is unchanged

checkpoint.explanation: What improved is how often instructions complete. Pipelining improves throughput, not latency. One instruction completes per cycle because five are in progress at once, not because any single one got faster.

checkpoint.prompt: Why does a 5-stage pipeline give only 3.6x on 10 instructions but 4.98x on 1000?

choices.A: The clock slows for short runs
choices.B: Ten instructions cannot fill five stages
choices.C: Short programs have worse cache behaviour
choices.D: The four cycles spent filling the pipeline are a large fraction of a short run and negligible in a long one

checkpoint.explanation: 4 + 10 against 50 is 3.6x; 4 + 1000 against 5000 is 4.98x. The same pipeline, with the fixed fill cost amortised differently.

checkpoint.prompt: Why did processor designs stop pursuing ever-deeper pipelines?

choices.B: A deeper pipeline discards more work when a branch is predicted wrongly, and that cost grows faster than the clock gain

checkpoint.explanation: Depth buys clock speed and pays for it in misprediction penalty. Beyond a point the penalty dominates, which is the calculation the exercise asks you to do.

checkpoint.prompt: Why must instruction memory and data memory be separate paths in a pipelined design?

choices.A: Fetch and the memory stage occur in the same cycle for different instructions

checkpoint.explanation: Both need memory access simultaneously. Two stages needing the same hardware in the same cycle would force one to wait. Separate paths — which in practice means separate first-level caches — remove that conflict.
